pack.title: Heat flow through layered building walls

provenance.notes: Layer dimensions and conductivities are chosen for this pack so that every numerical question depends on the supplied figure rather than on remembered material data.

blocks.text: Heat flow through layered building walls

When the two sides of a wall are held at different temperatures, heat flows steadily from the warmer side to the cooler one. In the steady state the rate of flow no longer changes with time, and the same quantity of heat passes through every layer of the wall each second. The flow is driven by the temperature difference across the wall and is opposed by the wall's thermal resistance.

blocks.caption: Figure 1. A single-layer wall. Heat passes from the warm side to the cool side at a steady rate.

blocks.latex: R = d / lambda;   Q = A * dT / R_total
blocks.caption: Thermal resistance of one layer, and the resulting rate of heat flow through the wall.

legend.meaning: thermal resistance of a layer per unit area, in square metre kelvin per watt
thickness of the layer in metres
conductivity of the layer's material in watts per metre kelvin

rate of heat flow in watts

blocks.text: A wall built from several layers behaves like a chain: the same heat passes through each layer in turn, and the resistances of the layers are added together to give the total resistance of the wall. Because the resistances are added, the order in which the layers are arranged does not change the total. A layer of low conductivity contributes a large resistance even when it is thin, while a thick layer of high conductivity may contribute very little.

blocks.caption: Figure 2. A two-layer wall of area 18 square metres, with the warm side held 20 kelvin above the cool side.

parts.label: Brick layer
parts.detail: thickness 0.24 m, conductivity 0.60 watts per metre kelvin

parts.label: Insulation layer
parts.detail: thickness 0.08 m, conductivity 0.05 watts per metre kelvin

blocks.text: Because the total resistance is a sum of positive terms, it is always larger than the resistance of any single layer taken alone. Adding a further layer can therefore only reduce the rate of heat flow, never increase it. Doubling the thickness of one layer doubles that layer's resistance, but it does not double the total resistance of the wall, because the other layers are unchanged.

Performance is usually quoted not as a resistance but as a U-value: the rate at which heat crosses one square metre of the wall for each kelvin of temperature difference, which is one divided by the total thermal resistance. Because it is stated per square metre and per kelvin, a wall’s U-value does not depend on how large the wall is or on how cold the day is. The guidance this text follows treats an external wall as adequate when its U-value does not exceed 0.28 watts per square metre kelvin.

questions.stem: Two external walls are built from the same two layers in the same thicknesses, but one is twice the area of the other. According to the text, how do they stand against the guidance?

options.text: The smaller wall is the more likely to be adequate, since less heat crosses it.
The larger wall is the more likely to be adequate, since its heat flow is spread over more area.
They stand identically, because the quantity the guidance limits does not depend on the wall’s area.
Neither can be judged until the temperature difference on the day is known.

supportSpans.quote: a wall’s U-value does not depend on how large the wall is or on how cold the day is

questions.explanation: The guidance is written against the U-value, and a U-value is stated per square metre of wall and per kelvin of temperature difference. Both of those are divided out, so two walls of the same construction have the same U-value whatever their size. More heat does cross the larger wall, but that is not the quantity being judged.

a.reason: Less heat does cross the smaller wall. The guidance does not limit the heat crossing a wall; it limits a rate stated per square metre, which is the same for both.

b.reason: The heat is not spread over more area in any sense that helps: the flow rises in proportion with the area, so the rate per square metre is unchanged.

d.reason: The temperature difference is divided out of a U-value as well, which is why the same limit applies whatever the weather.

hints.text: Find which quantity the guidance actually sets a limit on, rather than assuming it limits the heat flow.
The text says what that quantity is stated per, and that turns out to matter.
If a quantity is stated per square metre, doubling the square metres cannot change it.

questions.stem: What is the rate of heat flow through the wall shown in Figure 2?

supportSpans.quote: R = d / lambda;   Q = A * dT / R_total
thickness 0.24 m, conductivity 0.60 watts per metre kelvin
the resistances of the layers are added together to give the total resistance of the wall

questions.explanation: Each layer resists in proportion to its thickness and in inverse proportion to its conductivity: the brick gives 0.24 ÷ 0.60 = 0.4 and the insulation 0.08 ÷ 0.05 = 1.6, a total of 2.0. The wall is 18 square metres with 20 kelvin across it, so the flow is 18 × 20 ÷ 2.0 = 180 watts.

b.reason: 225 watts uses the insulation layer’s resistance alone. The brick resists as well, and the text says the layers’ resistances are added.

c.reason: 900 watts uses the brick layer’s resistance alone, which leaves out the layer carrying most of the resistance.

d.reason: 1125 watts divides by the two thicknesses added together. It is the resistances that are added, and a resistance is a thickness divided by a conductivity.

hints.text: Work out each layer’s resistance before you go near the heat flow.
The text says how the two resistances combine into one figure for the wall.
Then multiply the area by the temperature difference and divide by that figure.

questions.stem: In the wall shown in Figure 2, which layer contributes the greater share of the total thermal resistance, and why?

options.text: The brick layer, because it is the thicker of the two.
The insulation layer, because its conductivity is much lower.
The brick layer, because its conductivity is higher.
Both contribute equally, because the same heat passes through each of them.

supportSpans.quote: A layer of low conductivity contributes a large resistance even when it is thin, while a thick layer of high conductivity may contribute very little.
thickness 0.08 m, conductivity 0.05 watts per metre kelvin

questions.explanation: Resistance is thickness divided by conductivity, so a layer can win on either count. The brick is three times as thick, which pulls one way, but it conducts twelve times as well, which pulls much harder the other. Its resistance is 0.4 against the insulation’s 1.6, a fifth of the total against four fifths.

a.reason: Thickness is only the numerator. The text says directly that a thick layer of high conductivity may contribute very little, which is what happens here.

c.reason: Conductivity is the divisor, so a higher conductivity gives a smaller resistance. Being the better conductor is what makes the brick contribute less, not more.

d.reason: The same heat does pass through both layers, and that is precisely why their resistances add rather than average. Equal flow says nothing about equal resistance.

hints.text: Write down what a single layer’s resistance is made of before comparing the two layers.
The two layers differ in both quantities, and by very different factors.
Compare the ratio of the two thicknesses with the ratio of the two conductivities.

questions.stem: The brick layer in Figure 2 is replaced by one of the same material but twice as thick. Everything else is unchanged. By what factor does the rate of heat flow through the wall change?

options.text: It is unchanged, since the insulation carries the resistance.
It falls to about five sixths of its former value.
It falls to about one half of its former value.
It roughly doubles.

supportSpans.quote: Doubling the thickness of one layer doubles that layer's resistance
thickness 0.24 m, conductivity 0.60 watts per metre kelvin

questions.explanation: The brick resists 0.4 and the insulation 1.6, a total of 2.0. Doubling the brick’s thickness doubles its resistance to 0.8 and brings the total to 2.4. The area and temperature difference are unchanged, so the flow falls in inverse proportion to the total: 2.0 divided by 2.4, or five sixths.

a.reason: The insulation does carry most of the resistance, but not all of it. The brick’s share is a fifth, and doubling it moves the total.

c.reason: Halving would follow if the doubled layer were the whole of the wall’s resistance. The text warns that doubling one layer does not double the total.

d.reason: Adding resistance cannot raise the flow. The total resistance is the divisor, so a larger total gives a smaller flow.

hints.text: Work out the two layers’ resistances separately before changing anything.
Only one of the two changes, and the text says what happens to it.
The flow is inversely proportional to the total, so compare the old total with the new one.

questions.stem: Does the wall shown in Figure 2 meet the guidance the text sets?

options.text: Yes, comfortably.
Yes, though with very little to spare.
No; its U-value is nearly twice the greatest the guidance allows.
No; its U-value is more than ten times the greatest the guidance allows.

supportSpans.quote: treats an external wall as adequate when its U-value does not exceed 0.28 watts per square metre kelvin
thickness 0.08 m, conductivity 0.05 watts per metre kelvin

questions.explanation: The two layers resist 0.4 and 1.6, so the wall’s total resistance is 2.0 and its U-value is one divided by that, or 0.5 watts per square metre kelvin. The guidance allows no more than 0.28, and 0.5 is close to twice that. The wall does not meet it.

a.reason: A comfortable pass would need a total resistance well above 3.5. This wall reaches 2.0, and a larger U-value is a worse wall, not a better one.

b.reason: The wall is not marginal in either direction. Its U-value misses the limit by roughly the limit again, which is not a near miss.

d.reason: Ten times the limit would be a U-value of nearly 3, which is a total resistance of about a third. The insulation layer alone resists more than that.

hints.text: The guidance is written against a quantity the text defines from the total resistance; find it first.
Work out the wall’s total resistance, then turn it into that quantity.
Compare what you get with the greatest value the guidance allows, and by how much.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes would leave the wall in Figure 2 with a U-value no greater than the guidance allows?

options.text: Reversing the order of the two layers, so the insulation lies on the warm side.
Halving the area of the wall.
Adding a second insulation layer identical to the first.
Adding a second brick layer identical to the first.

supportSpans.quote: treats an external wall as adequate when its U-value does not exceed 0.28 watts per square metre kelvin
Because the resistances are added, the order in which the layers are arranged does not change the total.
thickness 0.08 m, conductivity 0.05 watts per metre kelvin

questions.explanation: A second insulation layer adds 1.6 to the wall’s 2.0, giving 3.6 and a U-value of about 0.278 — just inside the limit of 0.28. None of the others reaches it: a second brick layer adds only 0.4, and the remaining two changes do not alter the U-value at all.

a.reason: The text says the order of the layers does not change the total, because the resistances are added. Rearranging them changes nothing to be judged.

b.reason: A U-value is stated per square metre, so it does not move with the size of the wall. Half the wall would have half the heat flow and exactly the same U-value.

d.reason: A second brick layer adds only 0.4 to the total, taking it to 2.4 and the U-value to about 0.42 — still well above the limit. The brick is the layer that resists least.

hints.text: Two of the four changes can be dismissed without any arithmetic; find the sentences that dismiss them.
For the other two, work out what each adds to the wall’s total resistance.
Turn each new total into the quantity the guidance limits, and compare.
